context: Al-Ma’un is Makkan in the view of most scholars, though some held its later verses came down in Madinah around the hypocrites; the classical books record both. It opens with a question that sounds like an invitation to gossip, ara’ayta, have you seen the one who denies the din, the judgment and the religion, and then gives a description no one expected: not a man arguing philosophy, but a man shoving an orphan and never urging that the poor be fed. Denial, the surah insists, is visible at the dinner table before it is audible in debate.

Then the surah turns and does something even more unsettling for religious people: it pronounces woe upon some who pray, those heedless of their prayer, those who perform to be seen, and those who withhold al-ma’un, the small neighborly things, the pot, the bucket, the hand-tool, the salt, as Ibn Mas’ud and the early commentators explained. For the first community it fused creed, prayer, and kindness into one fabric that cannot be torn along convenient lines.
name_story: The surah is named for al-ma’un, the small borrowed helps of neighborly life named in its final verse, the things so minor that refusing them exposes a heart with nothing in it. Some early books cite it as Ara’ayta, have you seen, after its opening word, and some as Surat ad-Din, the surah of the judgment it opens with.

movements.note: The one who calls the judgment a lie is identified by conduct: he is the one who pushes the orphan away and does not urge the feeding of the poor.
The Quran’s most feared woe for worshippers: prayer performed but unminded, sahun, hearts absent and duties slack, hollow at the center.
The portrait completes: worship done for human eyes, and even the bucket and the pot refused, religion inverted into performance minus kindness.

themes.d: The surah tests belief in judgment not by questioning the tongue but by watching the hands: what a man does with orphans and food is his real theology.
Yadu’u al-yatim, he shoves the orphan: the treatment of the person who can repay nothing is the Quran’s recurring measure of a heart.
An salatihim sahun: not a missed prayer but an unminded one, kept as costume while its center, presence before Allah, has quietly died.
Yura’un: prayer aimed at human audiences is aimed away from Allah, and the surah lists it beside cruelty, not beside devotion.

themes.t: The smallest generosity as the largest sign
themes.d: Al-ma’un, the borrowed pot and bucket: a soul that cannot release trifles reveals what all its display was hiding.

heart: Al-Ma’un may be the most uncomfortable seven verses in the Quran for a practicing person, because its woe is aimed inside the mosque. Read slowly, it dismantles the quiet bargain many of us strike, ritual in exchange for exemption from character, and it starts with a scene anyone can picture: an orphan pushed aside by a man certain of his own respectability. The reciter is forced to ask not whether he prays, but where his prayer goes and what it produces; sahun, heedless, is a word that fits comfortable routines precisely.

The surah’s genius is its final word. It does not end with a cosmic image but with kitchenware, al-ma’un, the small things neighbors lend. Heaven, it turns out, watches the smallest transactions for the truth about the largest claims. Whoever finishes this surah honestly will do two things before the day ends: return his prayer to presence, and find one small, unglamorous kindness to complete, because in this surah that is what belief in the Day actually looks like.

passages.why: The question that redefines denial as something done to orphans before it is said about God.
The woe every praying person should hear at least once a week, aimed at hollow prayer.
The last word is a borrowed pot: the smallest kindness as the final test of the biggest claims.

connections.why: Ad-Duha commands, do not crush the orphan; Al-Ma’un shows the one who does, the command and its violation facing each other.
Al-Humazah indicts cruelty of the tongue and the hoard; Al-Ma’un indicts cruelty of the hand and the withheld bucket, two panels of one portrait.

virtue.text: No authentic hadith attaches a recitation reward to Al-Ma’un, and it needs no certificate: it is the Quran’s standing definition of religion that has lost its mercy, and reciting it honestly is itself a correction.
